findings.issue_text: [BUG] deleteByIDs uses strings.Repeat but the diff adds no "strings" import to xorm_store.go (only migrator is added), so the package fails to compile unless strings was already imported before this change. If strings is not already in the import block, the build breaks with 'undefined: strings'; every consumer of the annotations service fails to compile.

[ADVISORY] Successful cleanup batches are logged with r.log.Error at Error level, including the full ID list, on every batch of every cleanup cycle. Production error logs and log-storage costs are flooded with non-error per-batch dumps (tens of thousands of IDs for a 32767-size batch), and on-call responders will treat routine cleanup as an incident; should be Debug/Info.

[ADVISORY] The success-path log statement logs the err variable, which is always nil at that point, as an 'err' attribute, implying an error occurred. Log consumers filtering or alerting on err fields in Error-level lines will misfire on every cleanup batch.

[ADVISORY] The SQLite fallback comments a parameter limit of 999 but the guard uses sqliteParameterLimit=999 while the test exercises a 32767 batch; the branch triggers only when batch size > 999 even though the failing case is ids > 999 in a single statement, coupling the workaround to config rather than to actual len(ids). A future caller with batch size <= 999 but more than 999 ids in one batch cannot occur today, but the mismatched constants (999 vs SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER 32767 cited in the test name) make the real limit untraceable and invite an off-by-one when the constant is 'fixed'.

[ADVISORY] The new test case creates 40003 annotations (plus 80006 annotation_tag rows) via batched InsertMulti inside a single shared InitTestDB run and runs three full cleanup passes over them, in a test that only runs when -short is not set. CI wall-time for the integration suite grows substantially on the SQLite test backend (hundreds of thousands of individual INSERTs and DELETEs per run), making this test a likely candidate for timeout flakiness on slower runners.

[ADVISORY] fetchIDs selects IDs for the batch, then deleteByIDs deletes by those IDs in a separate statement, so concurrent inserts/deletes between the two statements mean the returned affected count no longer equals len(ids) and the loop terminates on a batch that deleted fewer rows than the LIMIT allowed, under-deleting until the next cycle. The comment acknowledges under-delete for inserts, but the same race also means untilDoneOrCancelled can spin an extra iteration or stop early with rows still matching the condition; acceptable per the stated tradeoff but the code logs count=len(ids) as 'cleaned', so operators cannot detect the divergence.

[BUG] The cleanup service ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, unconditionally running every registered cleanup job (temp files, short-lived tokens, annotation cleanup, etc.) 10x more frequently for all deployments, not just the annotation deadlocks this PR targets. All tenants on large instances execute the full cleanup sweep every minute, multiplying DB load and file-system scans; this reads as a debug leftover, not a reviewed default.

[ADVISORY] Normal per-batch cleanup progress is logged with r.log.Error at three call sites (lines ~529, ~551, ~563), including logging the nil err field and the full id slice. Every cleanup cycle emits Error-level logs in production, triggering alert noise on log-based error alerting; these are leftover debug statements that must be Info/Debug before merge.

[ADVISORY] Both cleanup tests were renamed to TestIntegration* and skip in -short mode, so the standard unit-test CI run no longer verifies any annotation cleanup behavior, including the previously-passing cases that were unit tests before this diff. A regression in CleanAnnotations (e.g., a broken SQL condition) passes the default CI suite and is only caught by the integration job; the new batch-size logic ships with zero short-mode coverage.

[ADVISORY] The new 40003-annotation batch test is gated behind integration mode only, so the exact scenario the deleteByIDs SQLite inline-ID path was written for (batch 32767 > parameter limit) is never exercised in the default test run. The inline SQL string-building branch (xorm_store.go deleteByIDs) can regress — e.g., malformed IN list — with no unit CI signal, defeating the purpose of the fix it validates.

[ADVISORY] deleteByIDs selects the inline-SQL branch based on r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize rather than len(ids), so a batch size above 999 always builds raw interpolated SQL even when the fetched id list is tiny. Not incorrect today, but the branch condition tests a different variable than the one that causes the failure (placeholder count = len(ids)); the next person tuning batch logic must know this coupling or introduce a SQL-injection-adjacent or incorrect-count bug.

[ADVISORY] fetchIDs guards against an empty condition with an error, but every call site builds condition via fmt.Sprintf that is always non-empty, making the guard dead code that suggests a safety property (no unconditioned table delete) the code does not actually enforce structurally. A future call site passing a condition assembled from optional parts (e.g., empty annotationType) silently bypasses the guard's intent; the check is in fetchIDs but the concatenation order means a whitespace-only condition also passes it.

[BUG] Routine per-batch cleanup progress is logged with r.log.Error (including the 'Annotations to clean by time', 'cleaned annotations by time', 'Annotations to clean by count', 'cleaned annotations by count', 'Tags to clean', 'cleaned tags' call sites) even on the success path where err is nil and y is nil. Every cleanup batch emits an ERROR-severity log line on a healthy system; operators with error-level alerting (or Grafana's own log-based alert rules) get paged every minute per batch, and real errors are buried in the noise.

[ADVISORY] The cleanup ticker interval is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which is unrelated to the stated 'database performance optimizations' intent and is not traceable to any requirement in the diff. All cleanup jobs (annotations, temp files, expired tokens/sessions depending on what Run dispatches) now execute 10x more frequently; on large instances this re-runs the very DELETE scans this PR is meant to make cheaper, and the behavior change is invisible to operators because no setting governs it.

[ADVISORY] TestAnnotationCleanUp is renamed to TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp with a testing.Short() skip, silently removing the default cleanup-behavior coverage from unit/short CI runs. A regression in the default-settings or max-count cleanup logic now passes every short-mode CI run; the only coverage for existing (pre-PR) behavior lives in tests that are skipped by default, so the deletion-loop rewrite in xorm_store.go is primarily validated only on long-mode integration runs.

[ADVISORY] The MaxCount branch's loop termination invariant changed subtly: the batch condition embeds ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT batch OFFSET MaxCount, and the offset is re-evaluated against a shrinking table after every DELETE batch. With concurrent inserts/deletes, the OFFSET window shifts between batches, so the loop can skip rows (under-delete, needing extra cycles) or delete rows inside the keep-window that shifted into the offset — the same race the comment for MaxAge explicitly accepts, but it is undocumented here and the old single-statement form had the offset computed once per statement.

[ADVISORY] The SQLite fast path in deleteByIDs uses fmt.Fprintf-style string interpolation of IDs (fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)) instead of parameters, and the declared limit of 999 contradicts the 32767 threshold exercised by the new test. IDs are int64s so injection is not currently exploitable, but the code establishes an interpolated-SQL pattern for an IN clause keyed on a runtime batch-size comparison (sqliteParameterLimit=999 vs SQLite >=3.32's 32767 limit asserted only in the test), so a future table/id-type change or a SQLite <3.32 deployment with a large configured batch size produces a statement exceeding the real parameter limit and fails at runtime.

[BUG] The cleanup service ticker is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute (time.Minute * 1), a 10x increase in cleanup frequency with no comment or config gate explaining it. All periodic cleanup work (tmp files, expired sessions/tokens, and the now-batched annotation cleanup loops) runs 10x more often in every deployment; if this is a debugging leftover it ships a 10x background-load regression that operators cannot tune back without a code change, since the interval is hardcoded.

[BUG] Normal, successful cleanup batches are logged via r.log.Error ("Annotations to clean by time", "cleaned annotations by time", "Annotations to clean by count", "Tags to clean", etc.), including the full id list and the raw cond string on every batch. Every cleanup cycle emits Error-severity log lines containing up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize (32767) ids each, per batch, per cycle — error-rate alerts page on routine behavior and log volume explodes; also the 'err' field logged is always nil because the error was already returned above, so the log asserts severity the outcome doesn't have.

[ADVISORY] The SQLite string-interpolation branch builds the IN-list by repeated fmt.Sprintf concatenation (values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)), which is O(n^2) in ids. With the new 32767-size batch (the exact case the new test exercises), building the SQL string performs ~500M character copies per batch on the cleanup path; a strings.Builder or single Sprintf over a slice avoids it. Next change to this branch also risks mixing the two formatting styles (fmt.Sprint vs %d) silently.

[ADVISORY] sqliteParameterLimit is hardcoded at 999 while the new test's own name documents that SQLite >= 3.32.0 allows 32767 parameters, so the driver-dependent fact lives in two places that can drift. The magic 999 vs the test's 32767 encode the same fact differently; if the limit comment/test is updated without the constant (or vice versa) the interpolation-vs-placeholder switch point silently diverges from the real driver limit, producing the very 'too many parameters' failure the branch exists to avoid on older SQLite builds.

[ADVISORY] Both annotation cleanup tests are renamed to TestIntegration* and skipped under testing.Short(), so the cleanup batching logic (the only nontrivial new code in this diff) has no coverage in short/CI-quick runs. A regression in fetchIDs/deleteByIDs/untilDoneOrCancelled (e.g. the under-delete-on-zero-affected path or the parameter-limit branching) ships green in short-mode CI and is only caught by the slower integration suite, if it runs at all for this package.

[ADVISORY] untilDoneOrCancelled terminates on zero affected rows, so when a fetched batch's rows are all deleted concurrently between fetchIDs and deleteByIDs the loop exits early and silently under-deletes for this cycle (acknowledged in the comment but also logged at Error level, conflating an expected race with a failure). Operators reading Error logs ('cleaned annotations by time', count=32767, affected=0) cannot distinguish the documented benign race from a real delete failure, since both surface identically at Error severity; the count-vs-affected mismatch is logged but not acted on or differentiated.

[ADVISORY] The MaxAge and MaxCount cleanup branches are now near-duplicate blocks (fetch IDs with a formatted cond, log, deleteByIDs, log, return), differing only in the cond string — the shared shape is hand-maintained twice including duplicated Error-level log calls. The next change to batching behavior (e.g. fixing the log level, adding a retry, or threading a per-batch metric) must be applied in three places (MaxAge, MaxCount, orphaned tags); the drift is already visible in this diff as each copy repeats the nil-err logging mistake.

[BUG] Routine cleanup progress is logged at Error level ('Annotations to clean by time', 'cleaned annotations by time', and the count branch equivalents) with the err field always nil on the success path. Every cleanup cycle on every Grafana instance emits multiple Error-level log lines for normal operation, paging on-call / tripping alert rules keyed on error logs and burying real errors; the intent of the original code (silent successful cleanup) silently drifted during review iteration without an accepted decision to make routine cleanup log at error severity.

[BUG] CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags also logs its per-batch 'Tags to clean'/'cleaned tags' progress at Error level with a nil err field. Every orphaned-tag cleanup pass produces Error-level log noise with err=<nil>, misleading operators into believing cleanup is failing.

[ADVISORY] The cleanup service tick interval was silently changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute inside a PR titled 'Database Performance Optimizations'. All cleanup jobs (tmp files, annotations, other sweeps) now run 10x more frequently on every instance; this increases DB and I/O load — the opposite of the stated intent — and the objective change was never surfaced as a decision point for reviewers; if the 1-minute value was meant only to speed up tests, it ships to production.

[ADVISORY] The SQLite >999-ID branch builds the IN-list with repeated fmt.Sprintf string concatenation, which is O(n²) in the number of IDs (up to batch size, e.g. 32767). For large batches on SQLite each cleanup batch pays quadratic string building and produces a giant un-parameterized statement; a perf PR introduces a new CPU/allocation hot spot on exactly the large-batch path it added tests for — strings.Builder or strings.Join would be linear.

[ADVISORY] The delete strategy was rewritten from a single atomic set-based DELETE ... WHERE id IN (subquery) to a non-transactional read-IDs-then-delete-by-IDs loop, changing cleanup semantics (visible window between SELECT and DELETE, under-delete on concurrent churn) with acceptance recorded only in a code comment. The original guarantee that a cleanup pass removed exactly the rows the subquery selected is gone: concurrent inserts/deletes between fetchIDs and deleteByIDs make affected counts differ from fetched IDs, so batch-loop termination and the reported 'affected' totals drift from what the old single-statement path reported; downstream callers/metrics comparing affected counts now see different values than before the change, with no explicit human sign-off of the semantic change.

[ADVISORY] TestAnnotationCleanUp was renamed to TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp (and TestOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst likewise) with a testing.Short() skip, silently demoting previously-default-run coverage to integration-only. Developers running the package with -short (the common fast inner loop, and any CI stage using short mode) now get zero coverage of the annotation cleanup logic whose production implementation this same PR substantially rewrote; the objective shift from 'unit-tested cleanup' to 'integration-only cleanup' was not an explicit review decision.

[ADVISORY] fetchIDs builds the SELECT via fmt.Sprintf with a caller-supplied condition that already embeds ORDER BY/LIMIT, and rejects an empty condition with an error that is unreachable from the three call sites, which always pass a non-empty condition. The table name and condition flow through string concatenation with the validation check dead in practice; the next caller that passes a table/condition pair gets no compile-time protection and the empty-condition guard only fires on a programming mistake, adding a branch that can never execute — a deletion-test candidate (fold the guard away or pass structured parameters).

[ADVISORY] Routine success-path cleanup work is logged via r.log.Error with the full ID list and condition string, e.g. `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err)`. Every cleanup batch (batch size configurable up to 32767, and the loop runs continuously in production every minute now that the cleanup ticker is 1 minute) emits an Error-level log line carrying thousands of IDs; operators' error telemetry/alerting is flooded with non-errors, and large `ids` slices are serialized into log lines, degrading log storage and obscuring genuine errors. Any log-based alerting on annotation-cleanup errors will fire constantly on healthy operation (three Error lines per batch across CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags).

[BUG] In the MaxAge cleanup loop, the batch's affected count is taken from `x` (rows deleted by deleteByIDs), so if rows are deleted between fetchIDs and deleteByIDs (e.g. a second Grafana instance in HA running the same cleanup job), the batch returns affected=0 and the retry loop terminates even though IDs were fetched and remaining matching rows still exist. In multi-instance deployments where each node runs the cleanup service, two instances racing on the same batch cause one to observe 0 affected rows and stop the whole MaxAge (and MaxCount) sweep early, leaving stale annotations that are only removed on a later cycle; combined with the code comment's acknowledged under-delete, this makes cleanup completion non-deterministic per run. The loop should terminate on `len(ids) == 0` (rows fetched) rather than on affected rows deleted.

[ADVISORY] The only tests covering the rewritten batched-deletion logic (TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp, TestIntegrationOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst) were renamed to Integration tests and now skip under `testing.Short()`, so in short-mode CI runs the new fetchIDs/deleteByIDs/untilDoneOrCancelled code paths have zero coverage. A regression in the new delete-by-ID batching (e.g., the placeholder-count mismatch or the SQLite string-interpolation path) passes the standard test run silently; only integration CI catches it, and developers running the default suite get false confidence.

[ADVISORY] The new code logs successful batch operations at Error level (r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", ...) and r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by time", ...) including "err", nil on every batch). Every cleanup cycle emits multiple Error-level log lines per batch (with full ID lists), triggering error-rate alerts and log noise for a normal, successful operation; operators will page on routine cleanup.

[ADVISORY] deleteByIDs switches to string-interpolated IDs only when batchSize > 999, but batch sizes between 1000 and 32766 on SQLite take the placeholder path with up to batchSize placeholders, which exceeds the 999-parameter limit the code comment itself cites on SQLite < 3.32. An operator setting AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize to e.g. 5000 on an older SQLite build gets a 'too many SQL variables' error on every cleanup batch; the new test only exercises the 32767 regime, leaving the 1000–32766 regime untested and broken under the code's own stated constraint.

[ADVISORY] The SQLite interpolation path builds the ID list by repeatedly re-wrapping a growing string with fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v), an O(n²) string concatenation over up to 32767 IDs. For the large-batch SQLite case the diff specifically targets, each batch burns quadratic CPU building the SQL string; with the new 1-minute cleanup ticker this repeats continuously. A strings.Builder or join would be linear.

[ADVISORY] The cleanup ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute with no corresponding test or configuration, and the annotation cleanup tests in this diff do not exercise the new frequency. Every Grafana instance now runs the (now much chattier, batched) annotation cleanup 10x more often; combined with the Error-level per-batch logging this multiplies log volume and DB load, and the change is untestable/untested in the diff.

[ADVISORY] The new SQLite-limit test case is itself gated behind the integration skip and only runs on whatever DB backend InitTestDB selects in that environment; the string-interpolation branch in deleteByIDs (batchSize > 999) is only reached when GetDBType() is SQLite, so on test databases running MySQL/Postgres the new branch is not exercised at all. The branch added specifically to fix the reported SQLite failure can still pass CI without ever executing; a syntax error in the interpolated SQL or the asAny conversion would only surface in production SQLite deployments.

[ADVISORY] Cleanup success paths log at Error level and dump the full ID list of every batch into the log message. Every cleanup cycle emits r.log.Error('Annotations to clean by time', 'ids', ids, ...) and 'cleaned annotations by time' even when the operation succeeds (err is nil), so operators' error dashboards/alerts fire on routine cleanup and large batches (batch size can be 32767) flood logs with thousands of IDs per cycle at 1-minute ticker frequency.

[ADVISORY] The delete of annotation rows is not paired with deletion of their annotation_tag rows, leaving orphaned tag rows after every cleanup batch. After any MaxAge/MaxCount deletion, annotation_tag rows for the deleted annotations remain until the separate CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags job runs in a later cycle; if that job errors or the instance is replaced before it runs, dangling tag rows persist and the tag-count assertions rely on the cleanup lag — previously the single-statement flow had the same gap but now the two-step select-then-delete widens the window between annotation and tag deletion.

[ADVISORY] The SQLite fast path interpolates IDs directly into the DELETE statement, bypassing parameterization based on a config comparison rather than the actual number of IDs fetched. The branch is chosen by comparing the configured batch size (r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize) to 999, not len(ids); when the batch size is set above 999 every SQLite delete — even one fetching 3 IDs — embeds values via fmt.Sprintf into raw SQL; IDs are int64s read from the DB so no injection today, but the statement-building path diverges from the parameterized path and any future change to the ID type or fetch query silently routes through string formatting.

[ADVISORY] untilDoneOrCancelled can terminate early (under-delete) whenever a fetched batch's rows are concurrently deleted before the DELETE runs, and the loop's termination signal is RowsAffected rather than 'no more matching rows'. If concurrent writes delete rows between fetchIDs and deleteByIDs, affected returns 0 and the whole cleanup loop exits even though matching rows remain; the code comment acknowledges this for inserts, but it applies to any concurrent delete too — leftover annotations survive this cycle and are only removed on the next scheduled run, so retention SLAs (MaxAge) can be temporarily exceeded.

[ADVISORY] Routine per-batch cleanup progress is logged at Error level (r.log.Error) including the full ID list, on a path that runs on every cleanup cycle and normally has err=nil. Every cleanup run of a large Grafana instance emits error-level log lines containing up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize (default config, up to 32767) IDs per batch, polluting error dashboards/alerts and producing multi-megabyte log lines; operators page on noise that is not an error.

[ADVISORY] The same Error-level logging pattern (with err always nil on the happy path) is repeated for the MaxCount and orphaned-tag cleanup loops. Same log-noise/misdirection consequence at each of the three loop sites: error-based alerting fires on every normal cleanup cycle, and the 'ids' dumps make log storage cost scale with cleanup batch size.

[ADVISORY] The cleanup ticker interval was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute with no accompanying comment or configuration, a 10x increase in cleanup frequency that looks like a local-testing leftover. All cleanup jobs (tmp files, annotation cleanup via the same service loop, expired tokens, etc.) run 10x more often in production, multiplying DB scan/delete load and making the newly-added per-minute annotation delete batches contend with inserts far more frequently — the exact deadlock condition this change restructures the code to avoid.

[ADVISORY] fetchIDs and deleteByIDs run in separate sessions/transactions with no locking, so concurrent deletes/inserts between the SELECT and the DELETE make affected < len(ids) silently. The comment acknowledges under-deletion for inserts, but a concurrent delete of an already-fetched ID makes the batch report fewer affected rows; since untilDoneOrCancelled terminates on affected==0, a batch whose rows were all deleted concurrently ends the whole loop early even though qualifying rows still exist — cleanup silently does less work than the reported total implies. Tolerable per the stated 'next cycle' rationale, but the loop-termination-on-zero-affected interaction means the next cycle may also see zero affected rows for the MaxCount case if the remaining rows fall under the OFFSET window.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] deleteByIDs selects the inline-SQL branch based on r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize rather than len(ids), so a batch size above 999 always builds raw interpolated SQL even when the fetched id list is tiny. Not incorrect today, but the branch condition tests a different variable than the one that causes the failure (placeholder count = len(ids)); the next person tuning batch logic must know this coupling or introduce a SQL-injection-adjacent or incorrect-count bug.

adjudication.rationale: In deleteByIDs, the SQLite inline-SQL branch is chosen by `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit` (and SQLite DB type), not by `len(ids)` (the actual number of placeholders/parameters). That’s not a correctness defect in this diff (IDs are `[]int64` coming from the DB via fetchIDs, so not user-controlled), but it is a real, diff-grounded maintainability/safety concern because the branching condition is coupled to configuration rather than the true parameter-count limit, and future tuning could unintentionally broaden use of raw-interpolated SQL.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The MaxCount branch's loop termination invariant changed subtly: the batch condition embeds ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT batch OFFSET MaxCount, and the offset is re-evaluated against a shrinking table after every DELETE batch. With concurrent inserts/deletes, the OFFSET window shifts between batches, so the loop can skip rows (under-delete, needing extra cycles) or delete rows inside the keep-window that shifted into the offset — the same race the comment for MaxAge explicitly accepts, but it is undocumented here and the old single-statement form had the offset computed once per statement.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims a subtle behavioral change in the MaxCount cleanup due to OFFSET being re-evaluated against a shrinking table “after every DELETE batch,” implying the old code computed the offset only once. But the pre-diff code already did repeated batched deletes via `executeUntilDoneOrCancelled(ctx, sql)`, which re-executed the same `DELETE ... LIMIT ... OFFSET cfg.MaxCount` statement in a loop, so the OFFSET window was also re-evaluated after each batch as the table shrank. The new code still re-evaluates the same `LimitOffset(batch, cfg.MaxCount)` condition per batch; the described shifting-across-batches behavior is not newly introduced by this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The SQLite fast path in deleteByIDs uses fmt.Fprintf-style string interpolation of IDs (fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)) instead of parameters, and the declared limit of 999 contradicts the 32767 threshold exercised by the new test. IDs are int64s so injection is not currently exploitable, but the code establishes an interpolated-SQL pattern for an IN clause keyed on a runtime batch-size comparison (sqliteParameterLimit=999 vs SQLite >=3.32's 32767 limit asserted only in the test), so a future table/id-type change or a SQLite <3.32 deployment with a large configured batch size produces a statement exceeding the real parameter limit and fails at runtime.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce a SQLite-specific branch in `deleteByIDs` that inlines the `ids` into the SQL string when `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999` (`values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)`), rather than using parameters. While the IDs are `int64` values sourced from `fetchIDs` (`SELECT id FROM ...`) so SQL injection is not currently plausible from what’s shown, it does establish an interpolated-IN-clause pattern and relies on a hardcoded/possibly outdated comment/limit (`sqliteParameterLimit = 999`) despite a new test using a much larger batch size (32767). However, the finding’s claim that a SQLite <3.32 deployment would fail due to exceeding the parameter limit is not supported by this diff, because the large-batch path avoids parameters entirely.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Normal, successful cleanup batches are logged via r.log.Error ("Annotations to clean by time", "cleaned annotations by time", "Annotations to clean by count", "Tags to clean", etc.), including the full id list and the raw cond string on every batch. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The SQLite string-interpolation branch builds the IN-list by repeated fmt.Sprintf concatenation (values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)), which is O(n^2) in ids. With the new 32767-size batch (the exact case the new test exercises), building the SQL string performs ~500M character copies per batch on the cleanup path; a strings.Builder or single Sprintf over a slice avoids it. Next change to this branch also risks mixing the two formatting styles (fmt.Sprint vs %d) silently.

adjudication.rationale: In xorm_store.go deleteByIDs(), the SQLite branch for large batches builds the IN-list via repeated `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop, starting from `fmt.Sprint(ids[0])`. This is a concrete, diff-grounded performance concern (not a correctness defect), and a `strings.Builder`/`bytes.Buffer` or pre-joined slice would avoid it.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] sqliteParameterLimit is hardcoded at 999 while the new test's own name documents that SQLite >= 3.32.0 allows 32767 parameters, so the driver-dependent fact lives in two places that can drift. The magic 999 vs the test's 32767 encode the same fact differently; if the limit comment/test is updated without the constant (or vice versa) the interpolation-vs-placeholder switch point silently diverges from the real driver limit, producing the very 'too many parameters' failure the branch exists to avoid on older SQLite builds.

adjudication.rationale: The diff hardcodes `const sqliteParameterLimit = 999` in `deleteByIDs` with a comment “SQLite has a parameter limit of 999”, while the newly added integration test explicitly names a different SQLite limit (“SQLite >= 3.32.0” and uses `annotationCleanupJobBatchSize: 32767`). However, it’s not a verifiable functional bug from the diff alone because the code’s behavior for large batches (like 32767) still avoids placeholders by inlining IDs, so it won’t trigger “too many SQL variables” failures in that case.

adjudication.rationale: The diff explicitly renames the unit tests to `TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp` and `TestIntegrationOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst` and adds `if testing.Short() { t.Skip(...) }` at the top of both. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] untilDoneOrCancelled terminates on zero affected rows, so when a fetched batch's rows are all deleted concurrently between fetchIDs and deleteByIDs the loop exits early and silently under-deletes for this cycle (acknowledged in the comment but also logged at Error level, conflating an expected race with a failure). Operators reading Error logs ('cleaned annotations by time', count=32767, affected=0) cannot distinguish the documented benign race from a real delete failure, since both surface identically at Error severity; the count-vs-affected mismatch is logged but not acted on or differentiated.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `untilDoneOrCancelled` is a generic loop that (by design) stops when a batch returns 0 affected rows, and the new cleanup flow is now `fetchIDs(...)` then `deleteByIDs(...)` per batch. In that pattern, it is possible for `fetchIDs` to return a non-empty `ids` slice while `deleteByIDs` returns `affected=0` (e.g., if those rows were deleted between the SELECT and DELETE), which would cause the loop to terminate for that run even though further matching rows might still exist. The diff also clearly logs expected/benign states at Error level regardless of `err` (`r.log.Error(..., "err", err)` after `err` is checked to be nil), so operators could see confusing Error logs like `count>0` with `affected=0` that are not actual failures. This is a concrete, diff-grounded observability/edge-case concern rather than a guaranteed functional break.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The MaxAge and MaxCount cleanup branches are now near-duplicate blocks (fetch IDs with a formatted cond, log, deleteByIDs, log, return), differing only in the cond string — the shared shape is hand-maintained twice including duplicated Error-level log calls. The next change to batching behavior (e.g. fixing the log level, adding a retry, or threading a per-batch metric) must be applied in three places (MaxAge, MaxCount, orphaned tags); the drift is already visible in this diff as each copy repeats the nil-err logging mistake.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows three very similar batched-cleanup loops using `untilDoneOrCancelled(...)` (MaxAge branch, MaxCount branch, and `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags`) that each build a `cond`, call `fetchIDs`, then `deleteByIDs`, with duplicated logging statements. Every cleanup cycle on every Grafana instance emits multiple Error-level log lines for normal operation, paging on-call / tripping alert rules keyed on error logs and burying real errors; the intent of the original code (silent successful cleanup) silently drifted during review iteration without an accepted decision to make routine cleanup log at error severity.

adjudication.rationale: In xorm_store.go, the new cleanup loops log routine progress with `r.log.Error(...)` on the success path in both MaxAge and MaxCount branches and in `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` (e.g., "Annotations to clean by time", "cleaned annotations by time", "Annotations to clean by count", "cleaned tags"). Every orphaned-tag cleanup pass produces Error-level log noise with err=<nil>, misleading operators into believing cleanup is failing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The SQLite >999-ID branch builds the IN-list with repeated fmt.Sprintf string concatenation, which is O(n²) in the number of IDs (up to batch size, e.g. 32767). For large batches on SQLite each cleanup batch pays quadratic string building and produces a giant un-parameterized statement; a perf PR introduces a new CPU/allocation hot spot on exactly the large-batch path it added tests for — strings.Builder or strings.Join would be linear.

adjudication.rationale: In `deleteByIDs`, the SQLite branch for `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999` builds the `IN (...)` list by repeatedly reassigning `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop. This causes repeated string reallocation/copying (quadratic-time growth) for large `ids` slices (e.g., the new test case sets batch size 32767), and also emits a very large un-parameterized SQL string. This is a diff-grounded, actionable performance concern rather than a correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The delete strategy was rewritten from a single atomic set-based DELETE ... WHERE id IN (subquery) to a non-transactional read-IDs-then-delete-by-IDs loop, changing cleanup semantics (visible window between SELECT and DELETE, under-delete on concurrent churn) with acceptance recorded only in a code comment. The original guarantee that a cleanup pass removed exactly the rows the subquery selected is gone: concurrent inserts/deletes between fetchIDs and deleteByIDs make affected counts differ from fetched IDs, so batch-loop termination and the reported 'affected' totals drift from what the old single-statement path reported; downstream callers/metrics comparing affected counts now see different values than before the change, with no explicit human sign-off of the semantic change.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly rewrites cleanup from single-statement set-based DELETEs (e.g., `DELETE FROM annotation WHERE id IN (SELECT ...)`) to a two-phase loop: `fetchIDs(...)` (SELECT) followed by `deleteByIDs(...)` (DELETE) inside `untilDoneOrCancelled(...)`. The comment in `CleanAnnotations` explicitly acknowledges changed semantics under concurrency (“may under-delete when concurrent inserts happen”), and since SELECT and DELETE occur in separate DB sessions there is a visible race window where concurrent churn can change what is deleted vs what was fetched. This also means `affected`/metrics can diverge from the old atomic-per-batch behavior. It’s an intentional tradeoff to avoid deadlocks, but it is a real semantic change worth explicit review/sign-off rather than only a comment.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] fetchIDs builds the SELECT via fmt.Sprintf with a caller-supplied condition that already embeds ORDER BY/LIMIT, and rejects an empty condition with an error that is unreachable from the three call sites, which always pass a non-empty condition. The table name and condition flow through string concatenation with the validation check dead in practice; the next caller that passes a table/condition pair gets no compile-time protection and the empty-condition guard only fires on a programming mistake, adding a branch that can never execute — a deletion-test candidate (fold the guard away or pass structured parameters).

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show `fetchIDs` assembling SQL with `fmt.Sprintf` and requiring a non-empty `condition`, and the three new call sites always pass a non-empty `cond`. However, the claim that the empty-condition guard is “unreachable”/“dead in practice” is not verifiable from this diff: `fetchIDs` is a new repository method that could be called by future/other methods (not shown), and the guard is a reasonable defensive check rather than a demonstrated defect. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Routine success-path cleanup work is logged via r.log.Error with the full ID list and condition string, e.g. `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err)`. Every cleanup batch (batch size configurable up to 32767, and the loop runs continuously in production every minute now that the cleanup ticker is 1 minute) emits an Error-level log line carrying thousands of IDs; operators' error telemetry/alerting is flooded with non-errors, and large `ids` slices are serialized into log lines, degrading log storage and obscuring genuine errors. adjudication.rationale: In xorm_store.go the new cleanup implementation logs routine, non-error control flow using `r.log.Error(...)` while `err` is often nil and the operation is expected in normal runs (e.g., inside the `untilDoneOrCancelled` callbacks for MaxAge/MaxCount and in `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags`). Those log lines also include the full `ids` slice and `cond` string, so with large batches (cfg allows `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` up to 32767 per the new integration test) this will emit huge Error-level messages repeatedly. adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] In the MaxAge cleanup loop, the batch's affected count is taken from `x` (rows deleted by deleteByIDs), so if rows are deleted between fetchIDs and deleteByIDs (e.g. a second Grafana instance in HA running the same cleanup job), the batch returns affected=0 and the retry loop terminates even though IDs were fetched and remaining matching rows still exist. In multi-instance deployments where each node runs the cleanup service, two instances racing on the same batch cause one to observe 0 affected rows and stop the whole MaxAge (and MaxCount) sweep early, leaving stale annotations that are only removed on a later cycle; combined with the code comment's acknowledged under-delete, this makes cleanup completion non-deterministic per run. The loop should terminate on `len(ids) == 0` (rows fetched) rather than on affected rows deleted.

adjudication.rationale: The new `untilDoneOrCancelled` loop is explicitly documented to stop when a batch returns “zero affected objects” (see the comment above `untilDoneOrCancelled`). In both MaxAge and MaxCount paths, the batch callback returns `x` from `deleteByIDs` as the affected count, not `len(ids)` fetched. If another instance deletes the same IDs after `fetchIDs` but before `deleteByIDs`, `len(ids)` can be >0 while `RowsAffected()` is 0, causing `untilDoneOrCancelled` to treat the sweep as “done” and stop without fetching the next batch of still-matching rows. This is a correctness issue grounded in the new fetch-then-delete logic in `CleanAnnotations`.

A regression in the new delete-by-ID batching (e.g., the placeholder-count mismatch or the SQLite string-interpolation path) passes the standard test run silently; only integration CI catches it, and developers running the default suite get false confidence.

adjudication.rationale: The diff renames the existing cleanup tests to `TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp` and `TestIntegrationOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst` and adds `if testing.Short() { t.Skip(...) }` at the top of both, meaning they will not run in `-short` mode. At the same time, the core cleanup implementation is significantly rewritten in `xorm_store.go` to use new batching helpers (`fetchIDs`, `deleteByIDs`, `untilDoneOrCancelled`) and a special SQLite path that inlines IDs when `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999`. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new code logs successful batch operations at Error level (r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", ...) and r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by time", ...) including "err", nil on every batch). Every cleanup cycle emits multiple Error-level log lines per batch (with full ID lists), triggering error-rate alerts and log noise for a normal, successful operation; operators will page on routine cleanup.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly introduces multiple `r.log.Error(...)` calls in `CleanAnnotations` and `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` for normal batch progress, e.g. logging counts/ids/cond and including an `"err"` field even when `err` is nil (before/after deletion). This will emit Error-level logs on successful cleanup cycles (potentially with large ID lists), creating alert/log-noise risk. It’s a real, diff-grounded operational concern, not a functional correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] deleteByIDs switches to string-interpolated IDs only when batchSize > 999, but batch sizes between 1000 and 32766 on SQLite take the placeholder path with up to batchSize placeholders, which exceeds the 999-parameter limit the code comment itself cites on SQLite < 3.32. An operator setting AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize to e.g. 5000 on an older SQLite build gets a 'too many SQL variables' error on every cleanup batch; the new test only exercises the 32767 regime, leaving the 1000–32766 regime untested and broken under the code's own stated constraint.

adjudication.rationale: In `deleteByIDs`, the SQLite fallback to string-interpolated IDs triggers whenever `r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999`. That means SQLite batch sizes in the 1000–32766 range (e.g., 5000) will *not* use the placeholder path; they will use the interpolation path and avoid exceeding the 999-parameter limit. Also, `fetchIDs` applies a SQL `LIMIT` based on the same batch size, so `len(ids)` should not exceed the configured batch size. The finding’s claim that 1000–32766 on SQLite “take the placeholder path” is contradicted by the condition in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The SQLite interpolation path builds the ID list by repeatedly re-wrapping a growing string with fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v), an O(n²) string concatenation over up to 32767 IDs. For the large-batch SQLite case the diff specifically targets, each batch burns quadratic CPU building the SQL string; with the new 1-minute cleanup ticker this repeats continuously. A strings.Builder or join would be linear.

adjudication.rationale: In `deleteByIDs` (xorm_store.go), the SQLite branch for `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999` builds a comma-separated `IN (...)` list by repeatedly doing `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop. This re-copies the growing string each iteration, yielding O(n²) time/allocations for large `ids` slices (the test adds a 32767 batch size case). This is a concrete, diff-grounded performance issue; it doesn’t directly break correctness but can waste CPU/memory. The mention of the 1-minute ticker is less directly tied to annotation cleanup, but the quadratic string build itself is verifiable.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The cleanup ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute with no corresponding test or configuration, and the annotation cleanup tests in this diff do not exercise the new frequency. Every Grafana instance now runs the (now much chattier, batched) annotation cleanup 10x more often; combined with the Error-level per-batch logging this multiplies log volume and DB load, and the change is untestable/untested in the diff.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the cleanup service ticker interval from 10 minutes to 1 minute (`pkg/services/cleanup/cleanup.go`: `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` → `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)`) with no accompanying configuration toggle or tests. Separately, annotation cleanup now does per-batch `r.log.Error(...)` logging inside `untilDoneOrCancelled` loops in `xorm_store.go`, which would amplify log volume if the job is scheduled more frequently. The integration tests added in `cleanup_test.go` focus on annotation deletion/batching behavior and do not exercise or assert anything about the cleanup scheduler frequency change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new SQLite-limit test case is itself gated behind the integration skip and only runs on whatever DB backend InitTestDB selects in that environment; the string-interpolation branch in deleteByIDs (batchSize > 999) is only reached when GetDBType() is SQLite, so on test databases running MySQL/Postgres the new branch is not exercised at all. The branch added specifically to fix the reported SQLite failure can still pass CI without ever executing; a syntax error in the interpolated SQL or the asAny conversion would only surface in production SQLite deployments.

adjudication.rationale: The added test case (`"should not fail if batch size is larger than SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER..."`) is inside `TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp`, which is skipped when `testing.Short()` is true, and it uses `db.InitTestDB(t)` without asserting the DB type. The new SQLite-specific logic in `deleteByIDs` only takes the string-interpolation path when `r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999`; on non-SQLite backends the test would exercise only the placeholder/asAny path, leaving the new SQLite workaround branch untested by this test. This is a concrete coverage gap for newly added nontrivial behavior, not a directly provable functional defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Cleanup success paths log at Error level and dump the full ID list of every batch into the log message. Every cleanup cycle emits r.log.Error('Annotations to clean by time', 'ids', ids, ...) and 'cleaned annotations by time' even when the operation succeeds (err is nil), so operators' error dashboards/alerts fire on routine cleanup and large batches (batch size can be 32767) flood logs with thousands of IDs per cycle at 1-minute ticker frequency.

adjudication.rationale: In xorm_store.go the new cleanup loops log with r.log.Error on the normal success path, including dumping full `ids` slices: e.g. inside the MaxAge branch `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, ... "err", err)` runs after `fetchIDs` even when `err == nil`, and similarly `r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by time", ... "err", y)` after delete. The MaxCount and orphaned tag cleanup paths do the same. This will mark routine cleanup as errors and can flood logs with thousands of IDs per batch (batch size can be 32767 per new test), and the ticker was reduced to 1 minute in cleanup.go, increasing frequency.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The delete of annotation rows is not paired with deletion of their annotation_tag rows, leaving orphaned tag rows after every cleanup batch. After any MaxAge/MaxCount deletion, annotation_tag rows for the deleted annotations remain until the separate CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags job runs in a later cycle; if that job errors or the instance is replaced before it runs, dangling tag rows persist and the tag-count assertions rely on the cleanup lag — previously the single-statement flow had the same gap but now the two-step select-then-delete widens the window between annotation and tag deletion.

adjudication.rationale: The diff still contains `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` (now also implemented via `fetchIDs` + `deleteByIDs`), and the tests assert `affectedAnnotationTags` returned from `cleaner.Run(...)`, which strongly implies tag cleanup is part of the same run path rather than “a later cycle.” The finding’s core claim (that tag rows necessarily remain until a later scheduled job and that assertions rely on lag) is not shown in the diff. While annotation deletions are not directly cascading to `annotation_tag`, that behavior existed before as well and the diff does not verify the claimed widened/unsafe persistence beyond the same run.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The SQLite fast path interpolates IDs directly into the DELETE statement, bypassing parameterization based on a config comparison rather than the actual number of IDs fetched. The branch is chosen by comparing the configured batch size (r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize) to 999, not len(ids); when the batch size is set above 999 every SQLite delete — even one fetching 3 IDs — embeds values via fmt.Sprintf into raw SQL; IDs are int64s read from the DB so no injection today, but the statement-building path diverges from the parameterized path and any future change to the ID type or fetch query silently routes through string formatting.

adjudication.rationale: In `deleteByIDs`, the SQLite branch chooses the non-parameterized SQL path based on `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999` (config) rather than `len(ids)` (actual placeholders needed): `if r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit { ... fmt.Sprintf(... ids ...) }`. This means when batch size is configured above 999, even small deletes will interpolate IDs into SQL instead of using placeholders. The finding’s point about diverging from parameterization is grounded in the diff; however, with `ids []int64` fetched from the DB (`fetchIDs` selects `id`), this is not a verifiable injection/security defect as-is, more of a robustness/maintainability concern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] untilDoneOrCancelled can terminate early (under-delete) whenever a fetched batch's rows are concurrently deleted before the DELETE runs, and the loop's termination signal is RowsAffected rather than 'no more matching rows'. If concurrent writes delete rows between fetchIDs and deleteByIDs, affected returns 0 and the whole cleanup loop exits even though matching rows remain; the code comment acknowledges this for inserts, but it applies to any concurrent delete too — leftover annotations survive this cycle and are only removed on the next scheduled run, so retention SLAs (MaxAge) can be temporarily exceeded.

adjudication.rationale: Diff changes cleanup to a two-step fetchIDs() then deleteByIDs() loop driven by untilDoneOrCancelled(), whose doc says it stops when a batch returns zero affected rows. In this design, if fetchIDs returns some IDs but those rows are concurrently deleted before deleteByIDs runs, deleteByIDs can return RowsAffected==0; untilDoneOrCancelled will treat that as "done" and stop without attempting another fetch that could still find other matching rows (next page of results). The comment in CleanAnnotations acknowledges potential under-deletion for concurrent inserts, but the same early-termination mechanism can also happen with concurrent deletes. This is a real, diff-grounded edge-case/behavioral concern, but it’s not clearly an unintended defect since the code explicitly accepts under-deletion and relies on future cycles.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Routine per-batch cleanup progress is logged at Error level (r.log.Error) including the full ID list, on a path that runs on every cleanup cycle and normally has err=nil. Every cleanup run of a large Grafana instance emits error-level log lines containing up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize (default config, up to 32767) IDs per batch, polluting error dashboards/alerts and producing multi-megabyte log lines; operators page on noise that is not an error.

adjudication.rationale: In xorm_store.go, the new batched cleanup logic logs routine per-batch progress using r.log.Error in multiple places (e.g., "Annotations to clean by time/count", "Tags to clean", and "cleaned ...") and includes the full `ids` slice in structured fields. These calls occur even when `err` is nil (the code logs before/after delete and passes `err`/`y` that are typically nil on success), and they are inside `untilDoneOrCancelled` loops that run every cleanup cycle. This is diff-grounded and could create noisy error-level logs and very large log entries for large batches, but it’s an operational/logging-level concern rather than a functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The same Error-level logging pattern (with err always nil on the happy path) is repeated for the MaxCount and orphaned-tag cleanup loops. Same log-noise/misdirection consequence at each of the three loop sites: error-based alerting fires on every normal cleanup cycle, and the 'ids' dumps make log storage cost scale with cleanup batch size.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds unconditional `r.log.Error(...)` calls in the happy-path cleanup loops for MaxAge, MaxCount, and orphaned-tag cleanup (e.g., in `CleanAnnotations`: `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time"... "err", err)` right after successful `fetchIDs`, and similarly for "...by count"; and in `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags`: `r.log.Error("Tags to clean"...)`). On success, `err` is nil, yet the log is emitted at Error level every batch, and it includes full `ids` slices, making log volume scale with batch size. This is a concrete, diff-grounded operational/logging concern but not a functional correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The cleanup ticker interval was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute with no accompanying comment or configuration, a 10x increase in cleanup frequency that looks like a local-testing leftover. All cleanup jobs (tmp files, annotation cleanup via the same service loop, expired tokens, etc.) run 10x more often in production, multiplying DB scan/delete load and making the newly-added per-minute annotation delete batches contend with inserts far more frequently — the exact deadlock condition this change restructures the code to avoid.

adjudication.rationale: The diff explicitly changes the cleanup loop ticker from `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` to `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)` in `pkg/services/cleanup/cleanup.go`, which will make whatever runs in that loop execute 10x more frequently. The diff does not add configuration, comments, or other safeguards to justify/limit this change, so the concern about increased production load and contention is grounded in the shown code change (even if the exact set of jobs in that loop isn’t fully visible in this diff).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] fetchIDs and deleteByIDs run in separate sessions/transactions with no locking, so concurrent deletes/inserts between the SELECT and the DELETE make affected < len(ids) silently. The comment acknowledges under-deletion for inserts, but a concurrent delete of an already-fetched ID makes the batch report fewer affected rows; since untilDoneOrCancelled terminates on affected==0, a batch whose rows were all deleted concurrently ends the whole loop early even though qualifying rows still exist — cleanup silently does less work than the reported total implies. Tolerable per the stated 'next cycle' rationale, but the loop-termination-on-zero-affected interaction means the next cycle may also see zero affected rows for the MaxCount case if the remaining rows fall under the OFFSET window.

adjudication.rationale: In the refactor, `untilDoneOrCancelled` stops when a batch returns `affected == 0`. But each batch does `fetchIDs` and `deleteByIDs` in separate `WithDbSession` calls (separate sessions/transactions). If concurrent activity deletes the fetched IDs between the SELECT and DELETE, `deleteByIDs` can return 0 affected even though the `ids` slice was non-empty and other qualifying rows still exist. That causes `untilDoneOrCancelled` to terminate early (because it keys off `affected`, not `len(ids)`), so cleanup can silently do less work than intended under concurrency. This behavior is directly implied by the new control flow in `CleanAnnotations`/`CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` and `untilDoneOrCancelled`.
